blocks.body: # What the current VLM prompt actually reveals

## Technical summary

The tool schemas reveal much of each task's static action graph—legal objects, sources, destinations, fixtures, and operations—but neither current prompt includes the saved symbolic initial state. A separate mismatch is visible below: SFT receives the natural-language task instruction while live evaluation currently receives only the composite-task name. Fix exact prompt parity before interpreting an initial-state inclusion A/B.

## Evaluation drops the natural-language instruction

The complete user messages differ only where their input sources differ at this initial turn. Evaluation is shorter because it substitutes the composite-task name for the natural-language instruction. Character count is only a compact indicator; inspect the exact messages below to judge semantic leakage from tool schemas.

## The Qwen chat template adds the missing output-format instructions

The earlier view separated the user message and function schemas, but the model sees both after Qwen's chat template inserts this wrapper into the system turn. Therefore the tool-call format is present in the actual tokenized request even though it is absent from the user message.

### Model-visible tool wrapper

```text
# Tools

You may call one or more functions to assist with the user query.

You are provided with function signatures within <tools></tools> XML tags:
<tools>
{one JSON function schema per available tool}
</tools>

For each function call, return a json object with function name and arguments within <tool_call></tool_call> XML tags:
<tool_call>
{"name": <function-name>, "arguments": <args-json-object>}
</tool_call>
```

## What is and is not disclosed

Tool allowlists often identify the only legal source and destination for required objects, which can act like a compact task graph. They do not disclose initial agent locations, open/closed access states, held objects, machine state, or scene-specific physical obstruction. The saved initial states are printed only as an audit appendix beneath each task and are not part of either model request.

## Recommended experiment

First make the full SFT and evaluation requests byte-identical at matched decision points. Then train and evaluate two otherwise identical arms: visual/history-only versus a compact public-state block containing the current agent's initial fixture and cabinet/drawer/fridge access states. Keep complete object locations out of the first A/B so it does not silently turn partial observability into a symbolic-state task.

## Limitations and open questions

These are exact initial-turn examples for two tasks, not an inventory of information leakage across all verified specifications. A repository-wide audit should classify which object-source and destination relations are uniquely determined by each tool schema before deciding whether the schemas expose too much.
